topic: The Fundamental Bridge: The Relationship Between Integrals and Derivatives

sections.title: Prerequisite Warm-up: The Tangent vs. The Area
sections.content: Briefly review the two main problems of Calculus: The slope of a curve (Derivative) and the area under a curve (Integral). Visualize them as 'Zooming in' versus 'Accumulating'.
sections.example: Visualize a bird flying: The derivative is its instantaneous velocity (a snapshot), while the integral is the total distance covered (the sum of all snapshots).

sections.title: The Inverse Mechanism: Cancellation
sections.content: Explain that integration and differentiation are inverse processes. If you take the derivative of a function and then integrate it, you return to the original state, akin to 'undoing' an operation.
sections.example: Imagine a robot moving along a line. Its position is f(x). Differentiation finds its velocity (f'). Integrating the velocity function retrieves the original position function f(x).

sections.title: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (Visualization)
sections.content: Introduce the connection using a graphical animation: An area function A(x) representing the area accumulated from a to x. Show how the rate of change of this 'area bucket' is exactly the height of the function at point x.
sections.example: A water tank filling up. The derivative of the 'Total Water Volume' (Integral) at any moment is exactly the 'Flow Rate' (Function) at that specific time.

sections.title: Practical Application & Summary
sections.content: Demonstrate that knowing the 'rate of change' (derivative) allows us to reconstruct the 'total accumulation' (integral) using the Anti-derivative. Summarize the link as the 'Fundamental Theorem of Calculus'.
sections.example: Use a character, 'Explorer Alex', who tracks their speed throughout the day. By integrating that speed graph, Alex can calculate exactly how many miles they traveled across the mountain range.
